query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Switching to an HVOF thermal spray process with an optimized standoff distance and a tailored powder size distribution will increase the deposition efficiency of the FeCoNiCrAl HEA bond coat, yielding a thicker coating (beyond the 15–45 μm baseline) while preserving coating integrity and maintaining minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy prepared from 15–45 μm feedstock deposited using the current thermal-spray method
generation.intervention: Adopt HVOF spraying with an optimized standoff distance and adjusted powder size distribution
generation.conditions: Deposition performed under controlled atmospheric conditions (low oxygen content) with HVOF parameters optimized for HEA feedstock; service conditions typical for thermal barrier coating bond coats (temperatures below ~1000°C) during both deposition and in-service operation
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced in-flight particle melting and densification resulting from higher particle speeds and controlled heating in HVOF, enabling better coating deposition efficiency while limiting oxidation
generation.mechanism: Under HVOF, faster particle velocities and a lower in-flight particle temperature compared to APS reduce oxidation, while the adjusted standoff distance and powder size distribution ensure more uniform melting and deposition. This promotes higher coating thickness without compromising adhesion or inducing excessive oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A statistically significant increase in coating thickness relative to the 15–45 μm baseline along with maintained or improved adhesion and minimal oxidation levels in the as-sprayed state
generation.baseline: 15–45 μm coating thickness achieved using the current thermal-spray process
generation.boundary: The effectiveness is expected under HVOF conditions with the specified optimized parameters; deviations in ambient oxygen levels or changes in powder characteristics may alter outcomes
generation.uncertainty: The precise increase in coating thickness and long-term performance under service conditions remain to be quantitatively determined, and powder-to-powder variability might affect reproducibility

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeCoNiCrAl HEA coatings on identical substrates—one using the current thermal-spray process and the other using the proposed HVOF process with optimized standoff distance and powder size distribution. Evaluate the coatings immediately after deposition and following simulated service conditions.
measurements: Coating cross-sectional thickness via scanning electron microscopy
Oxide content and composition using energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) or X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
Adhesion and integrity tests (e.g., scratch tests, micro-indentation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the HVOF-deposited coatings do not show a statistically significant increase in thickness compared to the 15–45 μm baseline or exhibit increased oxidation levels or degraded adhesion relative to coatings produced by the current method.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

Thus, in-flight oxidation of the AlCoCrFeNi particle during the spraying process can be beneficial for the tribological performance of the HEA coatings. Due to high specific surface area, the powder can oxidize differently from the cast bulk alloy. Moreover, the formation of multiple oxides—alumina, chromia, and spinel—changes the residual particle’s core composition and can lead to phase destabilization. Therefore, understanding the regularity of the oxidation behavior and phase transformation of the high-entropy powder at different conditions should be necessary for the production of a coating with high and determined property levels. In this work, the oxidation behavior and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder, produced via gas atomization, were studied. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and under prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 HVOF coatings were produced using various distances from the spray nozzle to the substrate to produce coatings with different oxide contents, and the coatings’ properties were investigated.

Oxidation and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder produced via gas atomization were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. The following was found:Under HVOF spraying, the processes of oxidation and phase transformations occur in the following sequence: (i) pronounced Al diffusion from subsurface BCC supersaturated solid solution to the particle surface; (ii) particle’s surface Al2O3 formation; and (iii) FCC formation in the Al-depleted subsurface layer.During continuous heating in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) Al diffusion to the surface; and (iii) simultaneous formation of Al2O3 and FCC due to Al outflow from BCC/B2.During prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) diffusion of Al, Cr, Fe, and Mo to the surface; and (iii) formation of surface Al2O3 and undersurface sigma due to enrichment of the undersurface zone with Cr

reading.lever: Adopt HVOF spraying with optimized standoff distance and adjusted powder size distribution to boost deposition efficiency and thickness.
reading.why: HVOF has proven to yield thicker, well-adhering HEA coatings with low oxidation, addressing the thickness shortfall while preserving integrity under service conditions.
